newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: South Korea LSWR demand seen stemming price slide.
newsitem.headline: South Korea LSWR demand seen stemming price slide.

text.p: Sudden demand from South Korea and loss of nuclear capacity in Japan could help stem the slide in low sulphur waxy residue (LSWR) prices in coming weeks.
But traders said the arbitrage to the west is closed so prices would still fall longer term because of a supply surplus.
LSWR, a fuel used for power generation, has dropped in value sharply since mid December after surging to a five-year high assessment on December 16 of $24.40 per barrel.
Late last week the product's value had fallen to $22.10.
But traders said the pace of the decline could slow in coming weeks.
South Korea's Korean Electric Power Corp (KEPCO) is to import 1.5 million barrels of LSWR in January and the same amount in February. It normally imports 500,000 to 600,000 barrels.
KEPCO is topping up its fuel needs to meet winter demand. It usually relies on liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports for fuel generation.
Japan, which on average imports less than one million barrels of LSWR, is expected to absorb around 1.2 million barrels in January, down from an estimated 1.6 million barrels in December.
Traders said current winter temperatures in Japan are higher than year-earlier levels, which is partly offsetting the loss of nuclear power capacity.

Several nuclear-generators of electricity have reported problems with plants since early November, helping the rise in LSWR prices. Some capacity remains down, which will support prices, traders said.
In the wider Asia market the demand/supply outlook points to a surplus of supply at a time when arbitrage sales to the west are not economical.
In January, India is expected to buy a usual 200,000 to 400,000 barrels and Italy its usual 600,000 barrels, traders said.
Traders assessed January demand for Asian LSWR at 3.7 million barrels.

But Asia's major exporter, Indonesia, allocated 3.5 million barrels for export in January. And traders said they expected state-owned Pertamina to make another export allocation for January of 500,000 barrels, which would take the total to 4.0 million.
Further demand might emerge from Australia, Taiwan, or the U.S., but that could easily be absorbed by supplies from Singapore and Malaysia, traders said.
The surplus would only be taken up once price fall low enough for western buyers.
One trader said LSWR needed to drop below $20.00 per barrel before cargoes could be lured west, otherwise freight costs made the trip too costly.
Current prices of alternative burning fuels like Minas, Widuri and Duri crudes were also expensive, traders said.
Minas was assessed at $23.05, Duri at $22.15 and Widuri at $22.85 -- all around their highest levels in five years.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-870-3082)
